lessons.title: Ratios and proportions
lessons.intro: A ratio a:b tells how many "parts" each quantity gets. A proportion is an equation of two ratios.
steps: Write the ratio as a fraction.
Find the size of one part.
Multiply by the number of parts you need.

examples.q: Ratio 3:5, 40 items in total. How many are in the first group?

traps: Don't mix up part-to-part (3:5) and part-to-whole (3:8).
Check the order in which the quantities are named.

practice.q: The ratio of boys to girls is 2:5. There are 15 girls. How many boys are there?
The ratio of boys to girls is 8:4. There are 32 girls. How many boys are there?
Paint and water are mixed in the ratio 7:4. The mixture is 132 liters. How many liters of paint are in it?
practice.why: 7+4 = 11 parts; one part = 12 L; paint = 7·12 = 84 L.

practice.why: 7+5 = 12 parts; one part = 15 L; paint = 7·15 = 105 L.

practice.q: Paint and water are mixed in the ratio 6:3. The mixture is 108 liters. How many liters of paint are in it?
practice.why: 6+3 = 9 parts; one part = 12 L; paint = 6·12 = 72 L.

practice.q: Solve the proportion x/2 = 27/18. What is x?
Solve the proportion x/5 = 48/20. What is x?
Solve the proportion x/3 = 24/24. What is x?

test.why: 6+4 = 10 parts; one part = 13 L; paint = 6·13 = 78 L.

test.why: 3+7 = 10 parts; one part = 12 L; paint = 3·12 = 36 L.

lessons.title: Percents
lessons.intro: A percent is one hundredth. On the SAT, percents appear in discounts, growth, taxes and shares.
formulas: Increase by p%: ×(1 + p/100); decrease by p%: ×(1 − p/100)
steps: Identify the whole (what the percent is taken of).
Turn the percent into a multiplier.
Multiply or divide — don't add percents to numbers by eye.

examples.q: A price rises 20%, then falls 20%. Result?
examples.a: ×1.2·0.8 = ×0.96 — 4% less than the original, not the same!

traps: Successive percent changes multiply; they do not add.
"Percent more than" is computed from the original number.

lessons.title: Linear equations
lessons.intro: A linear equation has the form ax + b = c. It is the most common topic in SAT Math.
formulas: ax + b = c ⇒ x = (c − b)/a, a ≠ 0
Fractions: multiply both sides by the common denominator
steps: Distribute and clear fractions.
Collect x on one side and numbers on the other.
Divide by the coefficient of x.
Plug the answer back in to check.
traps: Do the same thing to both sides.
A minus sign before parentheses changes every sign inside.
If x cancels: 0 = 0 means infinitely many solutions; 0 = 5 means no solution.
lessons.tip: Desmos: graph the left and right sides as y = … and find the intersection.

Solve: 9x + 14 = 59

Solve: x/2 + x/3 = 15

lessons.title: Word problems with linear equations
lessons.intro: The SAT likes to describe a situation in words: fees, wages, purchases. The key skill is turning words into an equation.
formulas: Total cost = fixed fee + rate·quantity (y = mx + b)
m is the rate of change (per 1 unit), b is the starting value
steps: Name the unknown with a letter.
Write what the total is made of.
Set up the equation and solve.
Answer the question that was asked (it may not be x itself).

examples.q: A membership costs $30 plus $5 per class; you paid $80. How many classes?

traps: The number without x in a model is the value when x = 0.
Read the question to the end — it may not ask for x.

practice.q: A taxi charges $23 plus $3 per mile. A ride cost $59. How many miles was the ride?
A taxi charges $27 plus $8 per mile. A ride cost $115. How many miles was the ride?
The equation y = 3x + 59 gives the cost y, in dollars, of printing x pages. What does 59 represent?
practice.why: When x = 0 the cost is 59 — that is the starting (fixed) fee.
opts: A fixed fee charged even for 0 pages

practice.q: The equation y = 3x + 31 gives the cost y, in dollars, of printing x pages. What does 31 represent?
practice.why: When x = 0 the cost is 31 — that is the starting (fixed) fee.
opts: A fixed fee charged even for 0 pages

practice.q: The equation y = 2x + 54 gives the cost y, in dollars, of printing x pages. What does 54 represent?
practice.why: When x = 0 the cost is 54 — that is the starting (fixed) fee.

practice.q: A student bought 12 notebooks, some for $6 each and the rest for $9 each, and paid $84. How many $9 notebooks did the student buy?
practice.why: Let y be the $9 notebooks: 6(12 − y) + 9y = 84 ⇒ 3y = 12 ⇒ y = 4.

practice.q: A student bought 10 notebooks, some for $3 each and the rest for $12 each, and paid $93. How many $12 notebooks did the student buy?
practice.why: Let y be the $12 notebooks: 3(10 − y) + 12y = 93 ⇒ 9y = 63 ⇒ y = 7.

practice.q: A student bought 7 notebooks, some for $2 each and the rest for $8 each, and paid $38. How many $8 notebooks did the student buy?
practice.why: Let y be the $8 notebooks: 2(7 − y) + 8y = 38 ⇒ 6y = 24 ⇒ y = 4.

test.q: The equation y = 4x + 27 gives the cost y, in dollars, of printing x pages. What does 27 represent?
test.why: When x = 0 the cost is 27 — that is the starting (fixed) fee.
opts: A fixed fee charged even for 0 pages

test.q: A student bought 12 notebooks, some for $6 each and the rest for $8 each, and paid $86. How many $8 notebooks did the student buy?
test.why: Let y be the $8 notebooks: 6(12 − y) + 8y = 86 ⇒ 2y = 14 ⇒ y = 7.

test.q: The equation y = 5x + 26 gives the cost y, in dollars, of printing x pages. What does 26 represent?
test.why: When x = 0 the cost is 26 — that is the starting (fixed) fee.
opts: A fixed fee charged even for 0 pages

test.q: A student bought 6 notebooks, some for $3 each and the rest for $7 each, and paid $30. How many $7 notebooks did the student buy?
test.why: Let y be the $7 notebooks: 3(6 − y) + 7y = 30 ⇒ 4y = 12 ⇒ y = 3.

lessons.title: Rates and unit rates
lessons.intro: A unit rate is how much of something there is per 1 unit (miles per hour, dollars per item).
formulas: Unit conversion: multiply by a fraction equal to 1 (e.g. 60 min / 1 h)
steps: Find the rate per 1.
Multiply by the amount you need.
Keep track of units.
traps: Average speed = total distance / total time, not the average of the speeds.
Minutes vs hours is a classic trap.

practice.q: A car travels at 60 miles per hour. How many miles does it travel in 5 hours?
A car travels at 64 miles per hour. How many miles does it travel in 5 hours?

practice.why: Rates add: 1/2 + 1/4 = 3/4 pool per hour ⇒ time = 4/3 h.

practice.q: One pump fills a pool in 4 hours; another fills it in 8 hours. Working together, how many hours do they take? (fraction)
practice.why: Rates add: 1/4 + 1/8 = 3/8 pool per hour ⇒ time = 8/3 h.

lessons.title: Exponents
lessons.intro: Exponent rules let you simplify expressions without a calculator.
steps: Rewrite with the same base.
Apply one rule at a time.
Compare exponents.
traps: (a + b)² ≠ a² + b².
A negative exponent does not make the number negative: 2^(−1) = 1/2.

lessons.title: Roots and radicals
lessons.intro: A root undoes a power. On the SAT you simplify radicals and solve simple radical equations.
steps: Pull perfect squares out of the radical.
In an equation, isolate the radical and square both sides.
Always check the solution.
traps: Squaring can create extra (false) solutions.

What is √4?

lessons.title: Statistics: mean and median
lessons.intro: Mean, median, mode and range describe a data set with one number.
formulas: Median = middle of the ordered list
steps: Order the data (for the median).
For "what must the next score be" problems, work with sums.

examples.q: The mean of 5 numbers is 12. Sum?
An outlier of 1000 in the set 10, 12, 14
examples.a: The mean jumps; the median barely changes.

traps: Find the median only in an ordered list.
With an even count, the median is the average of the two middle values.

steps: Count all outcomes.
Count the outcomes you want.
Simplify the fraction.
traps: Don't divide by the number of "other" outcomes (7/3 is wrong).
"At least one" is easiest as 1 − P(none).

lessons.intro: Core SAT geometry: areas of rectangles, triangles and trapezoids; perimeter. The formulas are on the reference sheet, but knowing them is faster.
formulas: If lengths are multiplied by k, area is multiplied by k²
steps: Sketch the figure and label it.
Split a complex figure into simple ones.
Check units (cm vs m).
traps: A triangle's height is perpendicular to the base — it is not the slanted side.

lessons.title: Inequalities
lessons.intro: Inequalities are solved like equations, with one important rule about the sign.
formulas: Multiplying or dividing by a negative number flips the inequality sign
a < x < b is a compound inequality
steps: Solve as if it were an equation.
If you divide by a negative, flip the sign.
In word problems, check whether the answer must be a whole number.
traps: Forgetting to flip the sign is mistake #1.
"Greatest number of tickets" — round down.

lessons.title: Slope of a line
lessons.intro: Slope tells how much y changes when x increases by 1.
formulas: y = mx + b (b is the y-intercept)
steps: Subtract the y-values in one order and the x-values in the same order.
Divide.
Check the sign: a line going up has m > 0.
traps: Horizontal line: m = 0; vertical line: slope is undefined.
Keep the same point order in numerator and denominator.

Interpret m and b in context.

steps: Make the coefficients of one variable match.
Add or subtract the equations.

traps: The answer is an ordered pair (x, y) — don't swap them.

lessons.intro: A function assigns exactly one output f(x) to each input x. The SAT tests evaluating, composing and reading graphs.

Compare coefficients.

lessons.title: Linear vs. exponential models
lessons.intro: How to tell a linear model from an exponential one, and compare their growth.
formulas: An exponential eventually overtakes any line
steps: Look at differences (linear) and ratios (exponential).
Compare values for several t.
traps: "By 5%" is exponential; "by 5 units" is linear.

practice.q: The number of subscribers increases by 300 every month. Which model fits?

practice.q: The number of subscribers increases by 40 every month. Which model fits?
practice.why: The same amount is added each time — linear.

practice.q: The number of trees in a park increases by 15% every month. Which model fits?
practice.why: It is multiplied by 1.15 each time — exponential.

practice.q: The number of bacteria increases by 8% every month. Which model fits?

practice.q: f(t) = 100 + 50t and g(t) = 100·(1.5)^t. What is the smallest integer t > 0 for which g(t) > f(t)?
practice.why: Try t = 1, 2, 3, …: at t = 2, g = 225 > f = 200 for the first time.

practice.q: f(t) = 200 + 100t and g(t) = 200·(1.5)^t. What is the smallest integer t > 0 for which g(t) > f(t)?
practice.why: Try t = 1, 2, 3, …: at t = 2, g = 450 > f = 400 for the first time.

lessons.title: Sampling, margin of error and conclusions
lessons.intro: Questions about studies: can the result be generalized, and can we talk about causes?
formulas: Random sampling ⇒ results generalize to the population
Larger sample ⇒ smaller margin of error
steps: How were participants chosen?
Was there random assignment?
Does the conclusion go beyond the data?

examples.a: The result can't be generalized to all city residents.

traps: Correlation ≠ causation.
Don't generalize to a group that wasn't sampled.

practice.q: To learn the opinion of all students at a school, it is best to survey:
practice.why: A random sample of the whole population avoids bias.
opts: a random sample of all students at a school
only people who volunteer to answer

practice.q: To learn the opinion of all students at a university, it is best to survey:
practice.why: A random sample of the whole population avoids bias.

only people who volunteer to answer

practice.q: A poll finds 38% ± 6% support a project. Which is a reasonable conclusion?
practice.why: The margin of error gives a plausible interval.

practice.q: A poll finds 52% ± 5% support a project. Which is a reasonable conclusion?
practice.why: The margin of error gives a plausible interval.

practice.q: A poll finds 70% ± 2% support a project. Which is a reasonable conclusion?
practice.why: The margin of error gives a plausible interval.
opts: The true share is likely between 68% and 72%

practice.why: Random assignment gives causation, but the sample wasn't random — don't generalize.
opts: Cause and effect — but only for participants like these
Cause and effect for everyone in the world

practice.q: A study used randomly selected adults from the whole country and then randomly assigned them to two groups. Which conclusion is justified?
practice.why: Random sampling + random assignment ⇒ causation, generalizable.
opts: A cause-and-effect conclusion that applies to the whole population sampled
A conclusion about one group only

practice.q: An experiment used students in one class, randomly assigned to groups. Which conclusion is justified?
practice.why: Random assignment gives causation, but the sample wasn't random — don't generalize.
opts: Cause and effect — but only for participants like these
Cause and effect for everyone in the world

test.why: Random sampling + random assignment ⇒ causation, generalizable.

A conclusion about one group only

test.why: The margin of error gives a plausible interval.

test.why: Random assignment gives causation, but the sample wasn't random — don't generalize.

lessons.title: Conditional probability
lessons.intro: P(A | B) is the probability of A given that B happened. In a table, "look only at row/column B".
formulas: In a table: cell / total of row (or column) B
steps: Find the condition (after "given", "if", "of the").
The denominator is the total of the condition group.
traps: P(A | B) ≠ P(B | A).

lessons.title: Mixed practice: hard problems
lessons.intro: Problems from all topics — like the second (harder) SAT module.
formulas: Review the formulas from earlier lessons
Time: about 1.5 minutes per Math question
steps: Identify the topic.
Pick the fastest method: algebra, Desmos, or plugging in choices.
Check that you answered the question asked.

practice.q: Solve x² + 7x + 10 = 0. Give the larger solution.
Solve: 8x − 14 = -30

lessons.title: Math test strategy
lessons.intro: Digital SAT Math: 2 modules of 22 questions, 35 minutes each. Module 2 is harder if module 1 went well.
formulas: Desmos is built in — use it for systems, parabolas and intersections
The reference sheet is always available
No penalty for wrong answers — never leave a blank
Student-produced responses: fraction or decimal, no units
steps: First pass: solve everything quick.
Mark long questions for review.
Second pass: the marked ones.
With 2 minutes left, answer everything.
traps: Don't spend 5 minutes on one question.
Re-read what is asked (x or 2x?).

practice.q: What is the vertex of y = (x + 4)² + 9?
x + y = 7 and x − y = 3. What is x?
What is the sum of the solutions of 2x² − 4x − 16 = 0?
5x + 3y = 7 and 3x + 1y = 9. What is the solution (x, y)?
practice.why: Elimination or Desmos: the lines meet at (5, -6).

y = 3(x − 4)² + 1. Which statement is true?
practice.why: a = 3 > 0: opens up, so the vertex is a minimum, y = 1.

Which equation is an exponential model?

lessons.title: Subject–verb agreement
lessons.intro: A verb agrees with its main subject noun, not with the nearest word.
formulas: a number of + plural; the number of + singular
steps: Find the verb.
Find the subject (cross out of-phrases and interrupters between commas).
Match the number.

examples.q: The group of researchers (is / are) ready.
examples.a: Cross out of researchers → group … is.

traps: Don't agree with the noun inside an of-phrase.
An interrupter between commas doesn't change the number.

practice.q: The list of names ___ on the desk.
The students in the back row ___ louder than the teacher.
Each of the paintings ___ painted by a different artist.
A number of scientists ___ questioned the results.
The collection of ancient coins, along with two rare maps, ___ displayed in the main hall.
practice.why: along with … is an interrupter; the subject collection is singular.

practice.q: Neither the manager nor the employees ___ aware of the change.
practice.why: neither … nor agrees with the nearer subject (employees) → were.

test.q: The report on the three surveys conducted last spring ___ that most residents support the plan.
test.why: The subject report is singular; surveys sits inside the on-phrase.

test.q: Among the most influential works of the period ___ a series of essays by Alice Dunbar-Nelson.
test.why: Inverted order: the subject a series (singular) comes after the verb.

lessons.title: Pronouns: case and clarity
lessons.intro: A pronoun must clearly point to one noun (its antecedent) and be in the right form.
formulas: Subject: I, he, she, we, they, who
Object: me, him, her, us, them, whom
it's = it is; they're = they are
Singular noun → it / its; plural noun → they / their
steps: Find what the pronoun refers to.
Check the number (it vs they).
If two nouns could fit, choose the option that names the noun.

examples.q: When Maya spoke to Lina, she …
examples.a: It's unclear who she is → name the person.

traps: its vs it's is a classic trap.
A company, team or country is it, not they.

practice.q: The company released ___ annual report in May.
Between you and ___, the plan won't work.
practice.why: After a preposition, use the object form: me.

practice.q: The birds returned to ___ nests at dusk.
The committee announced that ___ would delay the vote.
practice.why: A committee acting as one unit → it.

practice.q: After the scientists examined the fossils, ___ were sent to the museum.
practice.why: it could refer to the cat or the mouse — clarity is needed.

practice.q: The award was given to the student ___ essay was the most original.

test.q: When the cat chased the mouse across the shelf, ___ knocked over a vase.
test.why: Possession and clarity → the noun is named.

test.q: Researchers gave the volunteers a puzzle and a map; ___ was surprisingly difficult.
test.why: it/this could mean the puzzle or the map; the puzzle is clear.

lessons.title: Verb tense consistency
lessons.intro: A verb's tense must match the time of the events in the text.
formulas: Past: yesterday, in 1990, last year → simple past
Present perfect (has/have + V3): with since, for, experience up to now
Past perfect (had + V3): an action before another past action
steps: Find time markers and nearby verbs.
Keep the same tense unless there is a reason to change.
traps: Don't shift tense without a reason.
had + V3 only when there is a later past event.

practice.q: Yesterday, the team ___ the final match.
Since 2010, the city ___ three new parks.
By the time the firefighters arrived, the fire ___ out.
practice.why: Earlier than another past event → past perfect.

practice.q: Every summer, the festival ___ thousands of visitors.
practice.why: A regular, repeated action → simple present.

practice.q: In 1962, Rachel Carson ___ a book about the dangers of pesticides.
practice.why: In 1962 is a specific past time → published.

practice.q: The archaeologists dug carefully because they ___ that the site contained fragile pottery.

test.q: When the experiment ends next week, the researchers ___ data for six months.
test.why: Completed by a future moment → future perfect.

test.q: Before she became a novelist, Toni Morrison ___ as an editor for many years.
test.why: Earlier than another past event (became) → had worked.

lessons.title: Sentence boundaries: periods and semicolons
lessons.intro: Two independent clauses (ICs) can't be joined by a comma alone. That's a comma splice — the #1 punctuation error on the SAT.
formulas: IC, and/but/so IC (FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so)
A comma alone between two ICs is an error
steps: Check whether each part could stand alone as a sentence.
If yes, use a period, a semicolon, or a comma + FANBOYS.

examples.q: The sun set, the air cooled.
examples.a: Comma splice → The sun set; the air cooled.

traps: A semicolon works like a period: both sides must be complete sentences.
however after a semicolon needs a comma after it.

practice.q: Choose the correct punctuation: The museum opened in 1990___ it now hosts a million visitors a year.
The rain stopped___ the game resumed.
She studied all night___ she still felt unprepared.
The bridge was closed for repairs___ therefore, traffic was redirected.
Although the data were incomplete___ the team published its findings.
practice.why: The first part is dependent (Although) → comma.

practice.q: Coral reefs cover less than 1% of the ocean floor___ they support about a quarter of all marine species.
practice.why: Two ICs with no conjunction → semicolon.

test.q: The novel was rejected by six publishers___ it later became a bestseller.
Many desert plants store water in their stems___ others have roots that reach deep underground.

lessons.title: Colons and dashes
lessons.intro: A colon comes after a complete sentence, before an explanation, a list or an example.
formulas: Before a colon there must be a complete sentence
A dash can work like a colon at the end of a sentence
steps: Check that a complete sentence comes before the mark.
Does the second part explain the first?

examples.q: She had one goal: to win.
examples.a: A complete sentence before the colon, an explanation after it.

traps: No colon after include / such as / are.
A fragment can't come before a colon.

practice.q: The recipe requires three ingredients___ flour, sugar, and eggs.
The ingredients include___ flour, sugar, and eggs.
practice.why: After include, no punctuation is needed.

practice.q: He had only one fear___ public speaking.
The results were clear___ the new method was faster.
Scientists have long debated one question___ why do birds migrate at night?
The team faced a familiar problem___ there was not enough funding.
practice.why: The second part explains problem → colon.

test.q: Several animals, such as___ owls, bats, and moths, are active at night.
The architect's design had a single purpose___ to let as much light as possible into the building.

lessons.title: Commas: introductory elements and conjunctions
lessons.intro: Commas on the SAT: after an introductory element, before FANBOYS between two ICs, and in lists.
formulas: Introductory element, IC (After the game, we …)
No comma between a subject and its verb
No comma before FANBOYS if the second part is not an IC
steps: Find the main clause.
Set off the introductory part.
Check that you aren't splitting the subject from the verb.
traps: "The idea that he proposed, was …" — an extra comma between subject and verb.

practice.q: After the concert ended___ the crowd left slowly.
She wanted to travel___ but she had no money.
The museum displays paintings___ sculptures, and photographs.
The book that she recommended___ was fascinating.
practice.why: No comma between the subject and the verb.

practice.q: He finished the report___ and sent it to his manager.
practice.why: The second part has no subject — not an IC, so no comma.

practice.q: Hoping to see the comet___ the astronomers stayed up all night.

test.q: The study was small___ yet its findings changed the field.
Researchers who study sleep___ have found that teenagers need more of it.
test.why: who study sleep is essential (it identifies the researchers) — no comma.

lessons.title: Nonessential elements: commas, dashes, parentheses
lessons.intro: An element you can remove without losing the sentence's meaning is set off on both sides by matching marks.
formulas: The marks on both sides must match
Essential information (needed to identify who) takes no commas
steps: Remove the element in your head — is the sentence still complete?
Check that the marks come in matching pairs.

examples.q: My brother, a doctor, lives in Almaty.
examples.a: a doctor is set off by commas.

traps: Never a comma on one side and a dash on the other.
No commas around a name after "the writer" if there are many writers.

practice.q: Mount Everest___ the tallest mountain on Earth, is in the Himalayas.
The author — who grew up in Kazakhstan___ writes about the steppe.
The jaguar (a large cat native to the Americas___ is an excellent swimmer.
My friend___ Aigerim plays the dombra beautifully.
practice.why: Without the name we don't know which friend → essential information.

practice.q: The novel's narrator, a retired sailor___ tells the story in flashbacks.
practice.why: Opened with a comma → close with a comma.

practice.q: Biologist Rachel Carson___ wrote Silent Spring in 1962.
practice.why: Biologist + name is essential — no commas.

test.q: The festival — first held in 1987___ now draws visitors from around the world.
test.why: Opened with a dash → close with a dash.

test.q: The device, which runs on solar power___ can operate for weeks without charging.
test.why: which … is nonessential; close it with a comma.

lessons.title: Apostrophes and possessives
lessons.intro: An apostrophe shows possession (the dog's bone) or a contraction (it's = it is).
formulas: One owner: student's; many owners: students'
A plural without possession has no apostrophe
steps: Is there possession?
One owner or many?
traps: Plural ≠ possessive.
its' does not exist.

practice.q: The ___ tail was wagging.
All the ___ coats were in the hall.
The ___ toys were scattered everywhere.
practice.why: children is an irregular plural → children's.

practice.q: The city expanded ___ public transit system.
Several ___ were damaged in the storm.
The ___ findings surprised other scientists.

test.q: The artist's paintings and the ___ sculptures were displayed together.
Each ___ results were recorded in a separate notebook.

lessons.title: Parallel structure
lessons.intro: Items in a list or comparison must have the same grammatical form.
formulas: to swim, to run, and to bike (or swimming, running, and biking)
not only … but also …, either … or … — same form after both
Comparisons: To see is to believe
steps: Find the list or paired construction.
Identify the form of the first item.
Match the others to it.

examples.q: She likes hiking, swimming, and to read.

traps: Mixing -ing and to-infinitives is the classic error.

practice.q: She enjoys reading, writing, and ___.
The coach told us to stretch, to hydrate, and ___.
The job requires not only patience but also ___.
He would rather walk to school than ___ the bus.
The new policy aims to reduce costs, improve safety, and ___ more workers.
Volunteers spent the day planting trees, cleaning the river, and ___.

test.q: The study found that the drug was safe, effective, and ___.
For the ancient Greeks, the goal of education was to cultivate both the mind and ___.

lessons.title: Modifiers
lessons.intro: An introductory phrase describes whatever comes right after the comma. Otherwise you get a dangling modifier.
formulas: Walking to school, I saw … (I am the one walking)
After an introductory phrase, put the one doing the action
Place a modifier next to the word it describes
steps: Ask: who or what performs the action in the introductory phrase?
That word must come right after the comma.

examples.q: Walking to school, the rain started.
examples.a: The rain isn't walking → Walking to school, I got caught in the rain.

traps: Avoid options where an object or "it" follows the comma when a person did the action.

practice.q: Running down the street, ___.
Built in 1889, ___.
After finishing the exam, ___.
Known for her bold colors, ___.
practice.why: Frida herself is known, not her paintings.

practice.q: A pioneer in computing, ___.
opts: Grace Hopper's work led to COBOL
COBOL was developed with Grace Hopper

practice.q: Having studied the data carefully, ___.
opts: the conclusion was clear to the team
the team reached a clear conclusion

test.q: Native to the Andes, ___.
opts: farmers have grown quinoa for centuries
quinoa has been grown for centuries
test.why: Quinoa is native to the Andes.

test.q: Drawing on interviews with hundreds of workers, ___.
opts: the author offers a persuasive account

lessons.title: Logical comparisons
lessons.intro: Compare only comparable things: a painting with a painting, not a painting with a painter.
formulas: Her score was higher than John's (= John's score)
that of / those of replace the noun
Comparative for two, superlative for three or more
steps: Identify what is being compared.
Make sure the other side is the same kind of thing.

examples.q: Kazakhstan's area is larger than France.
examples.a: → than France's / than that of France.

traps: Trap: comparing a thing with a person or a country.

practice.q: My phone's battery lasts longer than ___.
The population of Tokyo is larger than ___.
Of the two essays, hers was the ___.
The climate of Almaty is milder than ___.
The poems of Abai are as widely read as ___.
Unlike most mammals, ___.
opts: eggs are laid by the platypus

test.q: The speed of light is far greater than ___.
Like the paintings of Monet, ___.
opts: soft light was used by Cassatt

lessons.title: Concision: cutting extra words
lessons.intro: If all options are grammatical, the right one on the SAT is usually the shortest that keeps the meaning.
formulas: Remove repeated meaning (return back, past history)
Remove empty phrases (due to the fact that → because)
steps: Compare the options by length.
Check that no meaning is lost.
Look for repetition.
traps: Don't pick a short option if it changes the meaning or breaks the grammar.

practice.q: She returned ___ to her hometown.
We postponed the meeting ___.
The final outcome ___ surprised everyone.
___, the team canceled the trip.
opts: Due to the fact that it was raining
Because of the fact of rain
Owing to the rain that was falling

practice.q: The museum, which is a building that was built in 1900, ___.
opts: is in need of being repaired
requires repairs to be done to it

practice.q: Each and every student must submit the form ___.
opts: by Friday at the latest deadline
on or before Friday's deadline date
no later than Friday as the deadline

test.q: The scientist proposed an approach that was ___.
test.why: new/novel/innovative mean the same; keep one word.

test.q: In the year of 1969, astronauts landed on the Moon ___.
opts: the first time ever in history

lessons.title: Transitions: contrast
lessons.intro: A transition shows the logical link between sentences. Contrast: the second idea goes against what the first leads you to expect.
formulas: Contrast: however, but, yet, nevertheless, still, on the other hand, in contrast, by contrast
steps: Read both sentences without the transition.
Identify the relationship: a contradiction?
Pick a word from that category.

examples.q: The plan was expensive. ___, it saved time.

traps: Choose a transition by logic, not by sound.

practice.q: The plan was expensive. ___, it saved a lot of time.
The test was difficult. ___, most students passed.
Cats are often independent. Dogs, ___, usually seek attention.
The weather forecast predicted rain. ___, the day was sunny.
The bridge was declared safe. ___, engineers continued to monitor it.
Most early critics dismissed the novel. ___, it is now considered a classic.

test.q: Some scientists argued the species was extinct. ___, a small population was discovered in 2019.
Solar panels are costly to install. Over time, ___, they reduce energy bills significantly.

lessons.title: Transitions: cause and effect
lessons.intro: The second idea is a result of the first.
formulas: Effect: therefore, thus, as a result, consequently, so, hence
steps: Check: does the second part follow from the first?
If yes, use a cause-and-effect transition.

examples.q: The road was icy. ___, the school closed.

traps: Don't confuse effect with addition (moreover).

practice.q: The road was icy. ___, the school closed.
She practiced every day. ___, she won the competition.
The factory closed. ___, hundreds of workers lost their jobs.
The plant received no sunlight. ___, it did not grow.
Bees pollinate many crops. ___, a decline in bees could threaten food supplies.
The new law lowered taxes on electric cars. ___, sales of such cars rose sharply.

test.q: Glaciers reflect sunlight. As they melt, less light is reflected; ___, the planet absorbs more heat.
The museum's collection outgrew its building. ___, the board voted to build a new wing.

lessons.title: Transitions: addition, example, sequence
lessons.intro: Besides contrast and effect, the SAT tests addition, examples, sequence and summary.
formulas: Addition: moreover, furthermore, in addition, also
Sequence: first, then, next, finally, subsequently
steps: Identify the role of the second sentence: example? addition? next step?
Pick a transition from that category.

examples.q: Many animals hibernate. ___, bears sleep through winter.

traps: Similarly only when a similar thing is described.
In fact strengthens or sharpens the previous idea.

practice.q: Many animals hibernate. ___, bears sleep for months.
The hotel is close to the beach. ___, it offers free breakfast.
First, mix the flour and sugar. ___, add the eggs.
Frogs absorb water through their skin. ___, some salamanders breathe through theirs.
The film was popular. ___, it became the highest-grossing film of the year.
The study had a small sample and lasted only a month. ___, its conclusions should be treated with caution.
practice.why: A summary of what was said.

test.q: Octopuses can open jars. ___, they have been observed using coconut shells as shelters.
Researchers first tagged the turtles. ___, they tracked the animals' movements by satellite.

lessons.title: Rhetorical synthesis: student notes
lessons.intro: You get bullet-point notes and a goal. Choose the sentence that accomplishes exactly that goal.
formulas: Read the goal in the question first (emphasize a difference, introduce, explain …)
The answer must match the goal precisely
The right option may not use every note
steps: Underline the goal.
Test each option: does it accomplish the goal?
True facts but the wrong goal = wrong answer.

examples.a: Choose the option with while / whereas / unlike.

traps: Don't pick the most detailed option — pick the one that meets the goal.

practice.q: Notes: The Nile is about 6,650 km long. The Amazon is about 6,400 km long. Goal: compare the lengths of the two rivers.
opts: The Nile (6,650 km) is slightly longer than the Amazon (6,400 km).
The Amazon is about 6,400 km long.

practice.q: Notes: Abai Kunanbayev was a poet. He translated Pushkin into Kazakh. Goal: introduce Abai to an audience unfamiliar with him.
opts: Abai Kunanbayev, a Kazakh poet, also translated Pushkin into Kazakh.
Pushkin was translated into many languages.

practice.q: Notes: Koalas eat eucalyptus. Eucalyptus is low in nutrients. Koalas sleep up to 20 hours a day. Goal: explain why koalas sleep so much.
opts: Because eucalyptus is low in nutrients, koalas sleep up to 20 hours a day to save energy.
Koalas sleep up to 20 hours a day.

practice.q: Notes: Study A used 50 participants. Study B used 5,000. Both found the same effect. Goal: emphasize a difference between the studies.
opts: Both studies found the same effect.
Study B was much larger than Study A, with 5,000 participants versus 50.

practice.q: Notes: Mars has two moons, Phobos and Deimos. Earth has one moon. Goal: emphasize a similarity.
opts: Both Earth and Mars have natural satellites.
Earth has one moon, while Mars has two.

practice.q: Notes: In 2015, a team discovered Homo naledi. Fossils were found in a South African cave. Goal: state where the fossils were found.
opts: Homo naledi fossils were found in a cave in South Africa.

test.q: Notes: Ginkgo trees existed 200 million years ago. They are now native only to China. Goal: emphasize the age of the species.
opts: Ginkgo trees, a species that existed 200 million years ago, are among the oldest living trees.

test.q: Notes: Novel X: 1950, 300 pages. Novel Y: 1990, 900 pages. Goal: contrast the lengths of the novels.
opts: At 900 pages, Novel Y is three times as long as the 300-page Novel X.

lessons.title: Words in context I
lessons.intro: Choose the word or meaning that fits the logic of the text.
formulas: Cover the blank and supply your own word
Clues: an explanation after a colon, an example, a contrast (but), a cause
A familiar word can have a different meaning in context
steps: Find the clue in the text.
Think of your own word.
Pick the closest option.

examples.q: The evidence was robust: several teams confirmed it.

traps: Don't choose a word because it "sounds smart".

practice.q: The evidence was ___: several independent teams reached the same conclusion.
Unlike her talkative brother, Dana is quite ___.

The usually ___ critic surprised readers by praising the film enthusiastically.
Because the instructions were ___, many users made mistakes.

test.q: The festival's popularity was ___; within five years, attendance had grown tenfold.
Although the treatment was promising in early trials, researchers remained ___ about its long-term effects.

lessons.title: Words in context II: academic vocabulary
lessons.intro: Hard SAT words appear in science and literature passages. Roots and tone help.
formulas: Common words: ambivalent, corroborate, mitigate, ubiquitous, tenuous, scrutinize, novel (new), arbitrary, pragmatic, substantiate
steps: Identify the tone of the passage.
Use word roots.
Put the option into the sentence and reread.
traps: novel as an adjective means "new", not "a book".

practice.q: New fossil evidence ___ the theory, providing strong support for it.
Plastic is now ___: it is found everywhere from mountaintops to ocean trenches.
The link between the two events is ___; there is very little evidence connecting them.
Planting trees can ___ the effects of urban heat by providing shade.
The author felt ___ about the city: she loved its energy but disliked its noise.
The team proposed a ___ approach that no one had tried before.

test.q: Rather than following a clear rule, the selection seemed ___.
Before publishing, editors ___ every claim, checking each source carefully.

lessons.title: Text structure and purpose
lessons.intro: Questions: "What is the main purpose of the text?" and "Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence?"
formulas: Purpose — why the author wrote it (explain, argue, describe, challenge)
Function — the sentence's role: introduce, give an example, counter, conclude
The verb in the answer must match what the text actually does
steps: Summarize the text in one sentence.
Identify what the author is doing.
Check the verb in each option.

examples.q: A text describes a theory and then raises an objection
examples.a: Purpose: present a view and then challenge it.

traps: Overly strong verbs (prove, refute) are often wrong.
A detail ≠ the main purpose.

practice.q: Text: 'Honeybees perform a waggle dance. The angle of the dance shows the direction of food.' Main purpose?
opts: To explain what information a bee's dance conveys

practice.q: Text: 'Many believe deserts are lifeless. In fact, the Sonoran Desert hosts over 2,000 plant species.' Function of the second sentence?
opts: It challenges the common belief with evidence
practice.why: It counters the belief with facts.

practice.q: Text: a scientist describes her method, then her results, then the limits of the study. Overall structure?
Text: 'Some historians claim the treaty failed. However, trade between the nations doubled after it was signed.' Purpose?
opts: To present a claim and offer evidence against it
To describe a treaty in detail

practice.q: In a passage about volcanoes, the sentence 'For example, Mount Tambora's 1815 eruption cooled global temperatures' functions to:
opts: Give an example supporting a general claim

practice.q: Text: 'The poem's speaker describes the sea in calm terms at first; by the end, the sea is violent and threatening.' This text mainly:
opts: Describes a shift in the poem's portrayal of the sea

test.q: Text: 'Researchers expected the new alloy to fail at high temperatures. Surprisingly, it remained stable above 1,000°C.' The second sentence:
opts: Presents a result that contradicts the expectation

test.q: Text: the author lists three reasons the city adopted bike lanes and ends by noting cyclist numbers tripled. Purpose of the final sentence?
opts: To show an outcome of the policy

lessons.title: Main idea
lessons.intro: Main idea = topic + central claim. It covers the whole text, not one detail.
formulas: The main idea is neither too narrow (a detail) nor too broad
Watch for but / however — the main idea often follows them
Put it in your own words before reading the options
steps: Read the text and find the repeated topic.
Find the turn (but).
State the idea and compare with the options.

examples.q: Early reports focused on cost, but later observations showed accessibility also mattered.

traps: only, all, never often signal a wrong option.
An option that repeats words from the text isn't necessarily right.

practice.q: 'Octopuses can solve puzzles, open jars, and recognize individual humans.' Main idea?
'Early reports on school gardens focused on cost, but later observations showed that accessibility also shaped success.' Main idea?
'Although electric cars produce no tailpipe emissions, manufacturing their batteries requires significant energy.' Main idea?
opts: Electric cars have environmental benefits and costs

practice.q: 'The steppe eagle, once common across Kazakhstan, has declined sharply due to power lines and habitat loss; conservationists are now insulating lines to protect it.' Main idea?
opts: A threatened eagle is the focus of conservation efforts

practice.q: 'Scholars long credited a single inventor with the printing press. Recent research, however, shows that similar technologies developed independently in Korea and China.' Main idea?
opts: The printing press was not important
Printing technology had multiple independent origins

practice.q: 'Sleep helps the brain clear waste products, consolidate memories, and regulate mood.' Main idea?
opts: Sleep has several important functions for the brain

test.q: 'Critics praised the novel's vivid setting, yet many found its characters flat and its plot predictable.' Main idea?
'While some ecologists view wolves solely as predators that reduce deer populations, studies in Yellowstone suggest wolves indirectly helped restore riverbank vegetation.' Main idea?
opts: Wolves may have broader ecological effects than once thought

lessons.title: Inference
lessons.intro: An inference is the most cautious conclusion that follows directly from the text's facts — usually "Which choice most logically completes the text?"
formulas: Inference = facts + the smallest logical step
may, might, suggests — cautious wording is often right
steps: List the facts.
Which conclusion is unavoidable?
Eliminate options that add new information.

examples.q: Weekend hours extended; weekend visits rose; weekday visits stayed the same.
examples.a: → weekend access may have contributed to the rise.

traps: Overly strong conclusions (all, always, proves) are wrong.

practice.q: The library extended weekend hours. Weekend visits rose; weekday visits stayed the same. This suggests that:
opts: Longer weekend hours may have increased weekend visits

practice.q: Plants in group A received fertilizer and grew taller than group B, which did not. Other conditions were identical. Researchers can conclude that:
Fossils of a sea creature were found on a mountaintop. Most likely:
A study found that people who drink more coffee live longer. The study did not control for income or exercise. Therefore:
opts: The study cannot show that coffee causes longer life

practice.q: Bird species X arrives at the lake two weeks earlier than it did 30 years ago; spring temperatures there have risen. The data suggest that:
opts: Warmer springs may be linked to earlier arrival
practice.why: A link, not a proven cause.

practice.q: Early manuscripts of the poem contain a stanza that later printed versions omit. Scholars therefore infer that:
opts: The stanza was removed at some point before printing
The poet never wrote the stanza
practice.why: It was in the manuscripts — so it was removed.

test.q: Researchers found pollen from a plant that grows only in warm climates in 5,000-year-old lake sediments in a now-cold region. This suggests that the region:
test.why: A conclusion about the past climate.

test.q: Two groups learned a skill: one practiced in a single long session, the other in several short sessions. A week later, the second group performed better. This suggests that:
opts: The first group was less talented

lessons.title: Textual evidence
lessons.intro: Question: "Which quotation/finding would most directly support the claim?" The answer is a detail that directly supports the claim.
formulas: Find the claim that needs support
The right option directly supports it — being on topic is not enough
steps: Restate the claim in your own words.
Test each option: does it support exactly this?

examples.a: Evidence: the count rose from 40 to 65.

traps: An on-topic option that isn't about the claim is a trap.

practice.q: Claim: the new schedule increased participation. Which finding supports it?
opts: Participation rose from 40 to 65 after the change

practice.q: Claim: the poet admired nature. Which line supports it?
Claim: the drug reduces symptoms. Which finding supports it?
opts: Patients on the drug reported 40% fewer symptoms than those on placebo

practice.q: Claim: sea otters help kelp forests. Which finding supports it?
opts: Where otters returned, sea urchins declined and kelp regrew

practice.q: Claim: the character is anxious about the future. Which quotation best supports it?
opts: 'She lay awake, wondering what tomorrow's letter would bring.'

practice.q: Claim: the tax cut did NOT increase spending. Which finding would most WEAKEN this claim?
opts: Spending rose 15% right after the cut
practice.why: A rise in spending contradicts the claim.

test.q: Claim: the ancient city traded with distant regions. Which finding supports it?
opts: Shells from a coast 1,000 km away were found in its markets

test.q: Claim: bilingual children are better at switching tasks. Which finding would most directly support it?
opts: In a task-switching test, bilingual children responded faster with fewer errors than monolingual peers

lessons.title: Evidence from tables and graphs
lessons.intro: Quantitative evidence: the text has a table or graph; choose the option that describes the data correctly AND supports the claim.
formulas: Read the claim in the text first
Check every number in the option against the table
The right option is both accurate and relevant to the claim
steps: Understand what the axes/columns show.
Find the claim in the text.
Eliminate options that misstate the data.
From the rest, pick the one about the claim.

examples.q: Claim: variety A yields more than B
examples.a: You need an option where A's yield > B's in the table.

traps: An option can be accurate but not about the claim.
Watch units and years.

practice.q: Table: City A — 2010: 50, 2020: 80. City B — 2010: 70, 2020: 60. Claim: City A grew while B shrank. Which choice supports it?
opts: A went from 50 to 80, while B fell from 70 to 60
practice.why: Both facts, and about the claim.

practice.q: Graph: Rainfall — May 20 mm, June 80 mm, July 30 mm. Claim: June was the wettest month. Which choice supports it?
opts: June's 80 mm exceeded May (20 mm) and July (30 mm)

practice.q: Table: Fertilizer X yield 5 t, Y 7 t, none 3 t. Claim: both fertilizers increased yield. Which choice supports it?
opts: X (5 t) and Y (7 t) both exceeded the unfertilized 3 t

practice.q: Table: Survey — 2018: 30% use bikes, 2022: 45%. Claim: bike use increased. Which choice is accurate and supports it?
opts: Bike use rose from 30% in 2018 to 45% in 2022

practice.q: Graph: Species A population 2000: 400, 2010: 250, 2020: 100. Claim: the population declined steadily. Best support?
opts: It fell from 400 to 250 to 100 over two decades

practice.q: Table: Group 1 (8 h sleep) test score 85; Group 2 (5 h) 70. Claim: more sleep was associated with higher scores. Which is accurate?
opts: Group 1, which slept 8 hours, scored 85 compared with 70 for Group 2

test.q: Table: Solar 2015: 2%, 2023: 9%; Coal 2015: 40%, 2023: 30%. Claim: solar's share grew even as coal's fell. Best support?
opts: Solar rose from 2% to 9% while coal fell from 40% to 30%

test.q: Graph: Plant height with music 12 cm, without 12 cm. Claim: music did not affect growth. Best support?
opts: Plants grew to the same height (12 cm) with and without music

lessons.title: Cross-text connections
lessons.intro: Text 1 and Text 2. Question: how would the author of Text 2 respond to Text 1?
formulas: Relationships: agreement, disagreement, agreement with a qualification, different emphasis
Look for agree, but, however in Text 2
steps: Claim of Text 1.
Claim of Text 2.
The relationship between them.

examples.q: Text 1: shared spaces are beneficial. Text 2: agrees but notes maintenance costs.

traps: A qualification ≠ complete disagreement.

practice.q: Text 1: Homework improves learning. Text 2: Homework helps, but too much causes stress. Text 2's author would most likely:
Text 1: Dinosaurs were cold-blooded. Text 2: Bone growth patterns show dinosaurs were warm-blooded. Relationship?
Text 1: Social media connects people. Text 2: Social media connects people across distances, strengthening long-distance friendships. Text 2:
opts: Extends Text 1 with a specific example

practice.q: Text 1: The ruins were a palace. Text 2: The ruins' layout fits a marketplace, not a palace. Text 2's author would likely say Text 1's interpretation:
opts: Overlooks evidence from the site's layout

practice.q: Text 1: Remote work raises productivity. Text 2: Productivity rose in some remote teams, but collaboration-heavy teams struggled. Text 2:
opts: Adds a limitation to Text 1's claim

practice.q: Text 1 argues a poem is about loss. Text 2 argues the same poem celebrates renewal. How would Text 2's author respond to Text 1?
opts: By offering a different reading of the poem

test.q: Text 1: A drug works well in mice. Text 2: Many drugs that work in mice fail in humans. Text 2's author would caution that:
opts: Results in mice may not apply to humans

test.q: Text 1: Urban gardens mainly provide food. Text 2: Urban gardens' main value is building community, with food a secondary benefit. Relationship?
opts: Text 2 shifts emphasis to a different main benefit

lessons.title: Literature and poetry
lessons.intro: Passages from novels and poems: understand the mood, the character's attitude and the role of details.
formulas: Descriptive details reveal a character's feelings
In poetry — images, repetition, shifts in mood
steps: Who is speaking and about what?
Which words carry the emotion?
Pick the option supported by specific words.

examples.q: 'The old house groaned in the wind, its windows dark.'
examples.a: The mood is gloomy and uneasy.

traps: Don't read in what isn't in the text.

practice.q: 'She smiled as she read the letter, then pressed it to her heart.' The character feels:
practice.why: A smile + pressed to her heart.

practice.q: 'The empty playground was silent, swings swaying with no one on them.' The mood is:
'He checked the clock for the tenth time, tapping his foot.' He is most likely:
In a poem: 'The river runs, the river sings, / the river carries quiet things.' The repetition of 'the river' mainly:
opts: Creates rhythm and focus on the river

practice.q: 'Grandmother's kitchen still smelled of bread, though she had been gone for years.' The tone is:
'Wonderful,' he muttered, staring at the flat tire in the pouring rain. The word 'wonderful' is used:

test.q: In a passage, a character repeatedly describes the city as 'a cage of glass and noise.' This suggests the character:
A poem begins with winter images and ends with buds opening. The shift mainly conveys:

lessons.title: Hard punctuation: all together
lessons.intro: Harder SAT modules mix every punctuation rule in long scientific sentences.
formulas: Find the main clause first (subject + verb)
IC + IC: semicolon, comma + FANBOYS, or period
Don't separate subject and verb, or verb and object
steps: Work out the sentence structure.
Apply the rule.
Check that the option doesn't break another part.

examples.q: The researchers, led by Dr. Lee___ published …
examples.a: Opened with a comma → close with a comma.

traps: A long sentence is not a reason to add a comma.

practice.q: The team, led by Dr. Akhmetova___ published its results in 2021.
The device was tested in three countries___ Kazakhstan, Brazil, and Kenya.

test.why: including … is set off by a comma.

lessons.title: Hard grammar: all together
lessons.intro: A mix of agreement, tense, pronouns and modifiers in complex sentences.
formulas: Find the subject through all the interrupters
Keep the tense consistent with the context
Put a modifier next to what it describes
steps: Figure out what the question tests (look at how the options differ).
Apply that rule.
traps: The differences between options reveal the topic of the question.

practice.q: The results of the experiment, conducted over three years, ___ published last month.
Each of the volunteers ___ a certificate after the project ended.
Having traveled across the steppe for weeks, ___.
opts: the city finally appeared to the explorers
the explorers finally reached the city

test.why: The subject (mirror and lamps) is plural; inverted order.

lessons.title: Reading & Writing test strategy
lessons.intro: Digital SAT R&W: 2 modules of 27 questions, 32 minutes each. Every question has its own short text.
formulas: Question order: words → structure → evidence → grammar → transitions → notes
